newsitem.title: SPAIN: Argentaria Q1 net seen down, but improvement ahead.
newsitem.headline: Argentaria Q1 net seen down, but improvement ahead.

text.p: Spain's minority state-owned bank Argentaria is expected to report a drop of 15.5 percent in first-quarter earnings on Wednesday, as the bank struggles to right itself strategically, analysts said.

A relatively strong first quarter a year ago will also make results look poor, although analysts predict strong full-year 1997 gains in comparison with last year when the group ploughed half its earnings back into a restructuring of its business.

On average, analysts polled by Reuters expected attributable profit at Spain's fourth-largest bank to fall to 18.91 billion pesetas from 22.39 a year earlier. Net interest income is seen edging up, with a slight decline in operating margin.
"We are not recommending the share...The bottom line is not going to be good unless they have solid financial results," said an analyst at a Spanish brokerage.
Argentaria, formed in 1991 in a merger of six state-owned banks and savings banks and still 29.2 percent state owned, boasted relatively strong results in the first quarter of 1996.
Earnings then were boosted by commissions growth from the state's sale of a 25 percent stake in the group and from a sale of bond holdings, analysts said.

That quarter was the last under Chairman Francisco Luzon. He was replaced by Francisco Gonzalez last May who shifted strategy to help cut a mountain of low-yielding assets and expensive liabilities and to expand a small domestic network.

"We expect a fall in net attributable profits of five to 10 percent because the year-ago quarter was Luzon's last and there were benefits from the privatisation," said Juan Berberana, analyst at AB Asesores in Madrid.

To help address its pressing problems, Argentaria said in December that it would devote nearly half its 1996 pre-tax profits to reduce the average interest rates on its liabilities and to shore up its balance sheet.
Last month, it introduced a new three-year plan aimed at boosting profitability and reinforcing its presence in the banking sector.
But this should have little immediate impact.
"They don't have much scope to improve (now) although obviously the end of the year will be better," an analyst said.
"Costs can't go down, they will grow as Argentaria builds up its network and they haven't worked out (Banco Exterior) BEX yet...The level of provisions can't go down (either)."

Subsidiary Banco Exterior's high costs and low profitability are seen as one of the bank's key problems, but one Argentaria is tackling and that should lead to enhanced profitability. "We believe that the heavy restructuring initiatives of 1996 will strongly underpin a sharp recovery in earnings growth in the next three years," said Morgan Stanley in an early April research report on Argentaria. It forecast the share would rise to 7,200 by the end of 1998 from the current 6,320.
